title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons
description:
Balloons are taped to a wall; balloon `i` spans the horizontal range `[xstart, xend]`. An arrow shot straight up at coordinate `x` bursts every balloon whose range includes `x` (endpoints inclusive), and keeps flying.

Return the minimum number of arrows needed to burst all the balloons.

examples.explanation: An arrow at x = 6 bursts [2,8] and [1,6]; an arrow at x = 11 bursts [10,16] and [7,12].
No two balloons share a coordinate.

hints: Each arrow should burst a group of balloons that all share a common point. How do you form the fewest such groups?
Sort by right endpoint. Shoot the first arrow at the smallest right endpoint: that balloon has to be burst, and shooting any further left cannot hit more balloons.
Every balloon whose start is <= the arrow position is hit. The first balloon that starts after it needs a new arrow at ITS right endpoint. Count arrows.
approach:
**Key insight: among the unburst balloons, the one with the smallest right endpoint must be hit by some arrow, and the best place for that arrow is exactly that right endpoint: any position further right misses this balloon, any position further left hits a subset of what the endpoint hits.**

Sort by `xend`. Shoot the first arrow at `points[0].xend`. Walk the list: a balloon whose `xstart <= arrow_x` is already burst (its `xend >= arrow_x` because of the sort order); the first balloon with `xstart > arrow_x` needs a new arrow, placed at its own `xend`. The number of arrows shot is the answer.

**Why it is correct (exchange argument):** take any optimal solution. Its leftmost arrow must hit the balloon with the smallest right endpoint `r`; moving that arrow to `r` still hits every balloon it hit before (they all contain `r` since they start `<= arrow <= r` and end `>= r`). Repeating on the remaining balloons shows the greedy never needs more arrows than optimal.

**Common mistakes:** sorting by start and trying to extend a running intersection without shrinking its right edge; using `>=` instead of `>` so that a balloon starting exactly at the arrow is treated as missed; integer overflow in languages with fixed-width ints when initialising `arrow_x` (use the first balloon's end instead of a sentinel).

**Interview follow-ups:** (1) This is the dual of Non-overlapping Intervals: arrows = size of the maximum set of pairwise disjoint balloons. (2) Each arrow has a width `w` (hits `[x, x+w]`): the same greedy with `arrow_x = end + w`. (3) Return the arrow coordinates, not just the count.
